text: This isn't a direct answer to your questions, but it's probably time to stop thinking about the Hot 100 chart as a gauge of what's "popular" or even "mainstream." It's performed that function less and less well over time. Streams and purchases of the entire history of recorded music pre-2026 plus all of the genres that don't have many new individual songs that make the chart are going to dwarf streams and listens of the Hot 100 at any given time. It's just math. If that's the case and most people are listening to songs outside the Hot 100, how much can it tell us about what's "popular?" It was a bigger indicator back when the backlog of popular recorded music was less vast and passive listening to radio programming shaped tastes more powerfully. Functionally, the Hot 100 is still a chart that tells us what new songs many, many people are listening to right now. But popularity is an increasingly different thing. And, like rock, hip-hop is now a popular legacy genre with an incomprehensibly massive audience whether or not tracks are charting. There are probably many, many more Americans who could tell you who Drake or even Biggie is than who Olivia Dean is (no shade to her!) That's not going to be captured there.

text: I mean, if you look at the greatest hits of Hall and Oates, and who has writing credits for them, according to Wikipedia, it's interesting. Hall and Oates are very much helped on a lot of the big hits by Sara Allen (Hall's longtime partner) and her sister Janna. She's Gone - Hall/Oates (Wikipedia quotes Oates saying he wrote the chorus and they wrote the verses together) Sara Smile - Hall/Oates Rich Girl - Hall Kiss On My List - Hall/Janna Allen (in an interview with Billy Corgan, Hall suggests that Janna Allen had the chorus, and they wrote the verses together) You Make My Dreams - Hall/Oates/Sara Allen (Wikipedia suggests that Oates had the feel and the title phrase, and Hall and Sara Allen fleshed it out) Private Eyes - Warren Pash/S. Allen/J. Allen/Daryl Hall - (Wikipedia quotes Hall as saying ""That's a real Janna Allen (co-writer and sister of Sara Allen) song. Janna, and I, and Warren Pash wrote that. Warren and Janna wrote most of the song, and I took it and changed it around ??changed the chords. Sandy (Sara Allen) and I wrote the lyrics. It's a real family song, the Allen sisters and me.") I Can't Go For That - S. Allen/Hall/Oates - according to Wikipedia, Hall came up with the feel and guitar riff, and Hall, Oates, and Allen worked on the lyrics. Did It In A Minute - Hall/S. Allen/J. Allen - according to Wiki, Janna Allen had the idea for the chorus, and Hall figured out some chords and a verse, and he wrote the lyrics with Sara Allen. Maneater - S. Allen/Hall/Oates - according to Wikipedia, it seems like Oates had a basic prototype of the song, and Sara Allen and Hall shaped its feel and the main hook Out Of Touch - Hall/Oates - Oates came up with the chorus, and then Hall and Oates wrote the verse together Method Of Modern Love - Hall/J. Allen Notably, Hall has a writing credit on every one of those songs, but the only song he has a sole writing credit for is 'Rich Girl' (and by the sounds, it's based on an experience of Sara Allen's, so maybe she should actually be credited for that too). So clearly he is most successful writing collaboratively, but was just as happy writing with his partner and her sister as Oates (or both). It actually looks fairly rare amongst these songs that Hall had the initial germ/idea of the song, for better or worse. Whereas, amongst these songs, Oates seems to most often come up with an idea, and then collaborates with Hall to flesh out the song, or Janna Allen has an idea that Hall fleshes out. Most Hall and Oates albums also do seem to have at least one song that was written and usually sung just by Oates (e.g., 'Mano A Mano' on Private Eyes, which I think is a pretty good song that could have been a single). So Oates clearly can do it himself if he wants. But he's also clearly aware Hall has the right voice for early 1980s pop, and that Hall has good pop instincts about that, and probably Hall wanted to tinker with things if he wanted to sing it. In terms of production, Hall and Oates do have production credits on most of their albums, and the early 1980s stuff is co-produced by Neil Kernon, who doesn't strike me as a David Foster-style "actually really the creative force" type producer, but instead is someone more of an engineer/practicalities kind of guy. So most likely, Hall and Oates were collaboratively coming up with the feels and details of the songs in the studio.
label: analysis

text: I have no specific knowledge of this partnership. But there are a lot of ways people can work together creatively. It's pretty common that most or all the notes in a song came from one person, but it may have taken the other person to lead them to it and bring it out of them. Take that away, and it may not happen. I was the second person in a band for many years. On some songs, he wrote the verses and all of the words, and I contributed the chords of the chorus. There were many others where he wrote all the parts. But it often started as a very vague idea that he would mumble or hum, and I'd play it back to him: "you mean like this?" And we worked together to bring it out, when though the content was all his. So when people say things like "it's all person 1, person 2 doesn't actually write anything," that might not be a useful or meaningful statement, even if it has some truth to it.
